claims.text: Surface segregation controls the premelting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface segregation controls the complete melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Inhibiting surface segregation through passivation will delay the onset of premelting relative to unmodified particles.
As-synthesized high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles possess intrinsic atomic-scale disorder in both their bulk and surface regions.
A selective surface-passivation treatment can inhibit surface segregation without altering the nanoparticle bulk composition.
The proposed behavior should be observable in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles smaller than 100 nm during controlled heating from sub-melting temperatures through complete melting.
Natural surface segregation produces low-cohesive-energy clusters at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-passivation treatment prevents the segregation-induced modification of surface atomic arrangements.
Segregation produces energetically favorable surface atomic arrangements that act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Passivation suppresses the formation of surface nucleation sites for premelting.
Suppressing surface premelting nucleation sites increases the thermal activation barrier for surface melting.
Passivated nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than unmodified nanoparticles.
Passivated nanoparticles will exhibit a delayed complete melting transition relative to unmodified nanoparticles.
Unmodified high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles naturally exhibit surface segregation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to nanoparticles used in typical catalytic and energy-related applications under controlled heating.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially larger particles or systems with different surface chemistries.
